tools.name: kanna_info
tools.description: Report which Kanna runtime this client is actually connected to. Returns the exact effective HTTP base URL and parsed host/port, client adapter identity, an allow-listed identity snapshot from the authoritative server /v1/status response, the separately advertised LAN endpoint, capability/write-path health, and an explicit serverStatus error when status cannot be fetched. The connected instance cannot be inferred from a default port, app path, display name, or process name.

params.name: machine_id
params.description: Machine id from kanna_list_machines. Omit it, or pass the current machine id, to use the local machine connected to this client.

tools.name: kanna_list_machines
tools.description: List the current Kanna machine and every sibling machine currently reachable through the signed-in account's relay connection. Use the returned machine id as machine_id on another tool to read or mutate that machine. The local machine is always returned; relayAvailable and error explain whether remote discovery is currently available.

tools.name: kanna_guide
tools.description: Read the Kanna manual for authoring repository config, workflows, agents, operating tasks, or making dev servers and visual companions available in Kanna Mobile (topic: mobile). The content comes from the running adapter's hot-reloadable tool catalog, so it matches the Kanna version exposing this tool.

params.name: topic
params.description: Manual topic to read.

tools.name: kanna_machine_stats
tools.description: Report current resource state for this machine and every reachable sibling machine: 1/5/15-minute load averages, CPU core count, memory used/free/available and macOS pressure when exposed, heavy build/test process counts (rustc, cargo, bazel, vitest, xcodebuild, and Node test runners), and open tasks whose runtimeState is busy. Results are observational and do not reserve capacity. Unreachable or incompatible peers appear in machineErrors and must be treated as unknown capacity.

tools.name: kanna_list_transfer_peers
tools.description: List the machines this Kanna machine can move a task to or from. The list is resolved in the server from its transfer peer registry and its provisioned cloud routes — the merge that used to exist only inside a signed-in desktop window — so an agent names a destination instead of scraping peer ids or relay credentials out of desktop code. Each entry carries peerId, the display name, and machineId when the machine is a same-account sibling whose cloud route this machine has provisioned; kanna_push_task and kanna_pull_task accept either spelling. transferable says whether a move can start right now and unavailableReason says what would make it possible. preferredTransport is "lan" whenever a LAN route exists, with cloudFallback for the same-account sibling reachable both ways. cloudRoute reports whether the cloud tunnel is usable: its Firebase credential is minted by the signed-in desktop app and can only be refreshed there, so a machine reachable only through an expired one is reported unusable here rather than accepted and failed later inside the transfer engine. Public keys and endpoints are deliberately absent. Pass machine_id to ask a sibling machine what it can reach before pushing a task from there.

tools.description: Register an existing local git repository with Kanna.

params.name: machine_id
params.description: Machine id from kanna_list_machines. Omit it, or pass the current machine id, to use the local machine connected to this client.

params.name: path
params.description: Absolute path to the local git repository to register.

params.name: name
params.description: Display name for the repository. Defaults to the directory name.

tools.name: kanna_reconcile_repo_metadata
tools.description: Detect a repository's authoritative default branch from origin HEAD, compare it with the recorded metadata, and update the existing repo record by default. This preserves the repo id and its tasks. Set apply=false for a doctor-style drift check without changing metadata. The response includes recorded and detected branch values, provenance for each, drift, and whether an update was made.

params.name: machine_id
params.description: Machine id from kanna_list_machines. Omit it, or pass the current machine id, to use the local machine connected to this client.

params.name: repo_id

tools.name: kanna_list_recent_tasks
tools.description: List recent Kanna tasks, newest first by update time. Inside a task session this defaults to that task's repository; pass all_repos for the rare cross-repository view. Set all_machines to discover tasks on every currently reachable account machine; that preserves the account-wide aggregation and returns tasks plus explicit machineErrors. Rows carry a prompt bounded to 500 characters, the latest durable agent name in agent, and the session transport in agentType.

params.name: machine_id
params.description: Machine id from kanna_list_machines. Omit it to use the connected machine, unless all_machines is true.

params.name: repo_id
params.description: Repository id to list on one machine. Inside a task session this defaults to the caller task's repository unless all_repos or all_machines is true. Cannot be combined with all_machines because repository ids are machine-local.

params.name: all_repos
params.description: List across repositories instead of applying the caller task's repository default. Cannot be combined with repo_id.

params.name: limit
params.description: Maximum rows per machine, clamped to 200. Defaults to 50.

params.name: all_machines
params.description: Aggregate tasks account-wide from the connected machine and every currently reachable sibling. Cannot be combined with repo_id because repository ids are machine-local. Every task row has machineId and unreachable peers appear in machineErrors.

params.name: include_closed
params.description: Include closed tasks as well as open tasks.

tools.name: kanna_get_task
tools.description: Fetch one Kanna task's detail. If the id is absent locally but exists on a reachable sibling, the error names that machine and tells you to repeat the call with machine_id. Returns: current workflow name (workflowName), stage, workspace branch (branch), pull-request URL (prUrl), worktree path, blockers, latest stage-run result (latestRun), the revision-round budget (revisionRounds, revisionLimit), and its place in the task tree — parentTaskId upward, childTaskIds downward. childTaskIds lists the task's direct children oldest first and includes closed ones, so a fan-out that lost the ids it created (compaction, a resumed session) rediscovers them here rather than re-listing the repo; a finished child is exactly the one an orchestrator must reconcile. Two independent state dimensions are reported. runtimeState is what the agent process is doing, straight from the daemon's terminal-state detection: 'busy' (working, including blocked inside a long tool or MCP call), 'waiting' (parked on an interactive prompt), 'idle' (settled at its composer between turns), 'exited' (its session ended without a replacement), or absent before any session reported one. readState is whether a human has read the latest output: 'read' or 'unread'. activity is the desktop's display value blending the two ('working' | 'idle' | 'unread') and is kept for existing consumers; it cannot answer either question on its own, because a busy agent nobody has read and a finished one both read 'unread'. Supervising a task means reading runtimeState: 'busy' is a live agent, never a parked one, whatever activity says. deliveredInputCount is how many messages have been delivered into this task's agent session from outside it — operator or manager kanna_send_task_input calls; historical counts may include retired completion notifications. Those messages are written to a live PTY, so a later stage running in a forked worktree with a fresh session cannot see them in any transcript it has: a non-zero count means an instruction history exists and kanna_task_inputs has its text. Never state that nothing was instructed, or that no owner input was sent, without reading kanna_task_inputs first. inputBlocked, when present, means the session is refusing every message delivered into it: 'inherited-draft-unknown' is a composer the daemon cannot prove is clear — a session adopted across a restart or handoff whose composer holds text nobody here saw typed, or one where a delivered message's text is parked unsubmitted — so submitting would append to an unsent line. It reads as a healthy idle task through activity and runtimeState; do not retry deliveries into it, and say plainly that a human has to resolve that terminal. The agent-facing view omits composer placeholders and suggestions unless the daemon's typed-byte ledger attests that a user actually typed the draft; any remaining composer field is therefore a real typed draft, not session output. Directives that were actually delivered are in kanna_task_inputs; what a task means is in its original prompt plus durable delivered directives.

params.description: Machine id from kanna_list_machines. Omit it, or pass the current machine id, to use the local machine connected to this client.

params.name: task_id
params.description: Task id (stable across stages) or one of the task's branch names (task-{id} or task-{id}-{n}).

params.name: agent_view
params.description: Sanitize provider-authored composer suggestions from agent-facing task detail. The catalog defaults this true; human UI callers use the ordinary unsanitized API view.

tools.name: kanna_list_task_children
tools.description: List this task's direct children only, including closed children, in chronological order. Each child exposes its workflow identity (workflowName), plus the agent and verdict from its latest recorded stage run; workflowName distinguishes runless specialty-review children from unrelated direct children. Use this durable history to join and reconcile a fan-out after notifications, compaction, or session resume; it is not an arbitrary closed-task listing.

params.description: Machine id from kanna_list_machines. Omit it, or pass the current machine id, to use the local machine connected to this client.

params.name: task_id
params.description: Task id (stable across stages) or one of the task's branch names (task-{id} or task-{id}-{n}).

tools.name: kanna_wait_task
tools.description: Block until a Kanna task finishes or closes, polling its detail. A task counts as finished once a termination is recorded: the task closed, its latest stage run reached a terminal status (succeeded or failed), or its agent session ended without a replacement (runtimeState 'exited'). It never resolves on read state, so a task whose agent is busy inside a long call and whose output nobody has read (activity 'unread') keeps the wait running, and a task whose agent stopped resolves whether activity settled to 'idle' or 'unread'. Returns the task detail plus waitOutcome 'resolved'; read the verdict from latestRun. If the wait window elapses first it returns the latest detail with waitOutcome 'timeout' instead of failing — that is a normal result, so call it again in a loop to keep waiting.

params.name: machine_id
params.description: Machine id from kanna_list_machines. Omit it, or pass the current machine id, to use the local machine connected to this client.

params.name: task_id
params.description: Task id (stable across stages) or one of the task's branch names (task-{id} or task-{id}-{n}).

params.name: timeout_secs
params.description: Seconds to wait before returning the latest detail with waitOutcome 'timeout' (clamped to at most 240, so the call returns inside the 300s tools/call timeout MCP clients enforce).

params.name: poll_secs
params.description: Seconds between polls (minimum 1).

params.name: until
params.description: 'finished' resolves when a termination is recorded — the task closes, its latest stage run reaches a terminal status, or its agent session exits; 'closed' resolves only when the task closes.

tools.name: kanna_wait_events
tools.description: Watch several Kanna tasks at once: blocks until any of them emits an event, then returns every event since your cursor plus a new cursor. This is the lossless fan-out primitive — kanna_wait_task blocks on one id and cannot supervise several tasks. Set include_current_activity for a level-triggered manager wait: after the fixed 10-second server debounce, a task already idle, waiting, or exited returns immediately as synthetic task.runtime_changed state, while short idle blips emit nothing. Scope it by task_ids, by parent_task_id (your own id, to watch everything you fanned out without naming it), by repo_id, or by the machine-independent repo_remote_url_hash. A repository-scoped wait issued from inside a task session excludes the calling task's own events by default — its KANNA_TASK_ID is added to exclude_task_ids — so a manager's own settled-runtime and activity edges never wake it; pass include_self true to receive them, or exclude_task_ids to drop other tasks from any scope. Event types: 'task.created', 'run.started', 'run.finished' (payload.status succeeded/failed/cancelled, payload.result), 'stage.changed', 'task.workflow_changed', 'task.pr_created', 'task.revision_requested' (payload.exhausted true means the task is parked for its human — stop waiting), 'task.closed', 'task.runtime_changed' (the manager signal: the daemon's own runtime verdict on the agent session moved between busy, waiting, idle and exited. payload carries previousRuntimeState, runtimeState and latestRunFinishedWithoutCompletion, whose true value identifies a parked task awaiting advance. Entering busy is published at once; every non-busy value must hold for a fixed 10-second server debounce, so busy/idle flicker emits nothing. This never encodes human read/unread state — watch it, not task.activity_changed, and drop the display event with exclude_event_types), 'task.runtime_settled' (deprecated: the busy-to-non-busy subset of task.runtime_changed, appended in the same transaction for watchers that already key on it), 'task.blocked' / 'task.unblocked' (the task acquired its first unresolved blocker, or lost its last one; payload.blockerTaskIds lists the unresolved blockers. Blocked is derived, so these also fire when a blocker task closes or reaches pr with a PR underneath a dependent), 'task.awaiting_advance' (a manual-stage main session exited without recording completion), 'task.awaiting_input' (the daemon positively identified an interactive prompt and the agent needs an answer, e.g. via kanna_send_task_input), 'task.activity_changed' (the human read/unread display dimension, not the manager one — a person reading a task moves it, so a manager should exclude it; provider-neutral and server-debounced on every activity direction for every provider; payload includes previousActivity, activity, runtimeState, and latestRunFinishedWithoutCompletion, whose true value identifies a parked task awaiting advance; no waiting-prompt placeholder or follow-up polling is required), 'task.merge_signaled' (the task's PR reached the repo's merge agent; payload.source is 'agent' or 'engine'), and 'task.merge_handoff_missing' (the workflow finished a stage that promised the merge handoff with no PR to hand off, so the task was NOT closed — treat it as a failed approval), 'task.raw_input_delivered' (discrete terminal keys or explicit bytes were written into the task's live PTY through kanna_send_task_raw_input; payload.writes lists each write's key name (null for explicit bytes), its exact bytes as hex, the declared composer class, and whether it was written, and payload.status is the call's verdict. These are actions, not speech: no task_input row exists for them and kanna_task_inputs will never show them), 'task.input_delivered' (a message was delivered into the task's agent session from outside it; payload.source is 'operator', 'manager', or 'unspecified' (historical retained events may carry 'notify'), payload.preview is a bounded prefix with payload.truncated saying whether it was cut, and the full text is readable with kanna_task_inputs), 'task.input_blocked' (the task's agent session started or stopped refusing messages delivered into it; payload.inputBlocked names the reason while it is blocked ('inherited-draft-unknown': the daemon cannot prove that composer is clear, because it adopted the session across a restart or handoff and its composer holds text nobody saw typed, or because a delivered message's text is parked unsubmitted there) and is null when it clears. The session is alive and idle the whole time, so nothing else in the feed says anything is wrong — but every delivery into it is refused, including the pre-close merge handoff, so stop sending and get a human to that terminal), 'task.teardown_failed' (detached workspace teardown failed to start or exceeded its deadline; payload.sessionId and payload.error identify the failure), 'task.lifecycle_operation_retired' (a durable post or stage-spawn intent was dropped without being applied because no server restart could ever reconcile it — an undecodable payload, an unknown kind, a payload naming another task, or a task closed underneath it; that intent is also the task's pre-operation guard, so this says the task was unblocked at the cost of the projection, with payload.reason, payload.operationId, payload.kind and payload.phase. An uncertain in-flight operation is never retired, and a retirement never destroys committed work: a stage spawn whose Spawn already crossed the daemon socket keeps the workspace it forked, because an agent may have run and committed there and the dropped stage move is what would otherwise have named it — payload.retainedBranch and payload.retainedWorktreePath are that branch and worktree, null when nothing was kept), and 'task.transfer_finalizing' (a cross-machine transfer is shutting the task's agent down so its conversation can be shipped; payload.phase is one of 'wrap-up-sent', 'idle', 'quit-sent', 'exited', 'already-exited', 'degraded'). Prompt text changing while a task remains idle or unread does not produce another event; read waitingPromptSnippet from kanna_get_task when reconciling a stopped task. Event payload fields describe the event-time fact: payload.stage is the stage then, and run events keep their own runId/status/result. Delivery-time state is separate under payload.currentTask (title, stage, activity, stageTransition, and latestRun for finished/awaiting events), so retained history cannot masquerade as today's failure. machineId identifies the source in the payload and aggregate row. Call it in a loop, passing back the short cursor handle you were given unchanged: events that fire between two calls are delivered on the next one, each exactly once. Omit the cursor on the first call to receive the retained history. A handle expires after 10 minutes without use or when its issuing process restarts; the returned error tells you to omit it and safely replay retained history. Legacy full cursor formats remain accepted and upgrade on resume. An elapsed window returns waitOutcome 'timeout' with no events — a normal result, not an error. Native fixed task/repo scopes use one sequence watermark. Native parent_task_id cursors bind that same global watermark to the parent id in a constant-size cursor; membership is evaluated at each read checkpoint, so reparenting never rewinds acknowledged events and newly eligible events after the checkpoint are delivered without cursor growth. hasMore true means another batch is already waiting, so call again immediately. Without machine_id, the connected kanna-server aggregates task, parent, and repository scopes across every sibling machine currently reachable through the account relay, tags every event with machineId, and returns machineErrors for stale or unreachable peers without advancing their native cursors; reconnecting peers catch up from retained history. Repository scope is matched by remote URL hash, not installation-local repo id. Per-machine checkpoints inside server ks1 and MCP km1 aggregates are emitted in one canonical ke1 envelope; deployed bare numeric, p3, kc1, and short-handle values remain accepted and normalize on resume. In kanna-mcp, the existing task_ids fan-in still covers tasks on different currently reachable machines and returns a short client-held aggregate cursor; legacy km1 aggregate cursors remain accepted. A machine_id pins the entire wait to one machine. Each MCP call remains clamped to 240 seconds so clients that abort tools/call around 300 seconds do not discard its result. For an arbitrarily long push-equivalent manager wake, run `kanna-cli task watch` as a background process; it loops this same feed, owns cursor hygiene, and exits when actionable work arrives.

params.name: machine_id
params.description: Machine id from kanna_list_machines. Omit it, or pass the current machine id, to use the local machine connected to this client.

params.name: task_ids
params.description: Task ids (or branch names) to watch, e.g. the child tasks you created. Required unless parent_task_id or repo_id is given.

params.name: parent_task_id
params.description: Watch every task fanned out under this parent instead of naming ids: pass your own task id and you get your children's events without remembering what you created. Re-resolved on every call, so a child created after you started watching is in scope on the next one. Direct children only, and the parent's own events are excluded — the same set kanna_get_task reports as childTaskIds. Ignored when task_ids is given; takes precedence over repo_id.

params.name: repo_id
params.description: Watch every task in this local repository and matching copies on sibling machines. Inside a task session an otherwise unscoped wait defaults to the caller task's repository. The server resolves this installation-local id to the repository's remote URL hash. Ignored when task_ids or parent_task_id is given.

params.name: repo_remote_url_hash
params.description: Watch matching repository copies on every machine by the remoteUrlHash returned from kanna_list_repos. Use this when no local repo id is available. Ignored when task_ids, parent_task_id, or repo_id is given.

params.name: exclude_task_ids
params.description: Task ids (or branch names) whose events are dropped from whichever scope was chosen. A filter, not a scope: it is not part of the cursor, so adding or removing an exclusion never invalidates a checkpoint, and an id that matches no task excludes nothing. Inside a task session a repository-scoped wait adds the calling task's own id here automatically unless include_self is true.

params.name: exclude_event_types
params.description: Event type names dropped from whichever scope was chosen — the way a manager opts out of noise it will only discard. A filter, not a scope: it is not part of the cursor, so changing it never invalidates a checkpoint, and an unknown name drops nothing. Filtering happens in the server, so the wait does not return at all for a dropped event. A manager watching runtime state passes 'task.activity_changed' (and 'task.runtime_settled' if it keys on the superseding 'task.runtime_changed'), so a human merely reading a task's output never wakes it.

params.name: include_self
params.description: Set true to keep the calling task's own events in a repository-scoped wait issued from inside a task session (for example to observe your own run.finished). Consumed by the client; it only disables the automatic self-exclusion and never touches explicit exclude_task_ids entries.

params.name: local_only
params.description: Keep this request on the selected machine and return its native cursor. Used by compatibility adapters that already aggregate per-machine waits; ordinary callers should omit it.

params.name: include_current_activity
params.description: Make the wait level-triggered for manager activity. In addition to durable events, return an immediate synthetic task.runtime_changed row for every scoped task already idle, waiting, or exited for the fixed 10-second server debounce. Short idle blips emit nothing. This uses daemon runtime state only, never human read/unread activity, so a restarted manager cannot miss parked work. Synthetic rows share the response limit with durable events; pass the opaque cursor back and drain while hasMore is true to page every settled task exactly once for that cursor. Keep this true while shepherding tasks; after servicing or deliberately ignoring a still-idle task, remove that task from an explicit task_ids scope.

params.name: short_cursor
params.description: Return a short durable cursor handle instead of the legacy encoded checkpoint. Keep this enabled for agent use. Active watchers reuse one handle, and the handle survives server and relay reconnects for the task-event retention window.

params.name: from
params.description: On a cursorless first call, set this to 'now' to establish the durable event checkpoint at the current tail. With include_current_activity true, already-settled scoped tasks are still returned as synthetic current-state rows. Omit it to preserve the retained-history replay contract. Once a cursor exists, the cursor is authoritative.

params.name: cursor
params.description: Short cursor handle returned by the previous call; pass it back unchanged. It independently checkpoints durable sequence progress and include_current_activity settled-row paging on every machine, so durable events arriving between pages are not lost. Omit on the first call to receive retained history and current settled state for the scope. Legacy full cursors remain accepted.

params.name: timeout_secs
params.description: Seconds to block before returning waitOutcome 'timeout' with no events (clamped to at most 240, so the call returns inside the 300s tools/call timeout MCP clients enforce).

params.name: limit
params.description: Maximum durable plus synthetic rows in one response (1-500, default 100). hasMore true means at least one native or aggregate-machine continuation remains; call again immediately with the returned cursor until hasMore is false.

tools.name: kanna_notify_mobile
tools.description: Send an operator-facing push notification to Kanna Mobile through the relay. Delivery to registered devices reports status (accepted, deliveryFailed, or noRegisteredDevices), acceptedCount, failedCount, and token-free provider failure reasons. A noRegisteredDevices result is live, never cached, and carries noDevicesReason: code neverRegistered (no phone ever registered for this account), unregistered (the mobile app retired the registration at retiredAt), tokenRejected (the push provider rejected the token as providerCode during a delivery from retiredByDesktopId at retiredAt), or unknown, plus an operator-facing message. Treat noRegisteredDevices as the operator being unreachable by push right now: do not retry the same message, report the reason to the operator through the task and your summary, and tell them to open Kanna on the phone while signed in so it re-registers. Use this for meaningful long-running-task milestones or when the operator needs to act. When task_id is present, tapping opens that task.

Revision rounds already spent carry over, and changing a workflow does not change the repo's sticky creation-time workflow choice.

tools.name: kanna_task_inputs
tools.description: Read a Kanna task's durable instruction history: every message delivered into its agent session from outside that session, oldest first. Each record carries the full message text, the time it was delivered, the stage and stage run that were live when it landed, and a caller-declared source — "operator" (a human, or their words relayed), "manager" (an orchestrating agent on its own authority), "unspecified" (the client declared nothing), or historical "notify" rows from the retired completion-injection path. These messages are written to a live PTY and appear in no transcript a later stage inherits, so this is the only durable place they exist: a review stage or dispatcher runs in a forked worktree with a fresh session and must read this before making any claim about what was or was not instructed. total is the full count and inputs is the most recent tail window, so a truncated window is visible rather than silent. Stage prompts, post prompts, and revision feedback are not here — they are already durable on the task's stage runs.

params.name: machine_id
params.description: Machine id from kanna_list_machines. Omit it, or pass the current machine id, to use the local machine connected to this client.

params.name: task_id
params.description: Task id (stable across stages) or one of the task's branch names (task-{id} or task-{id}-{n}).

params.name: tail
params.description: Maximum number of most-recent records to return, clamped to 500. Defaults to 100.

tools.name: kanna_task_transfers
tools.description: Read every machine-to-machine transfer this machine recorded for a task, newest first. This is the durable answer to whether a scheduled move actually happened: kanna_push_task and kanna_pull_task only queue intents, and the engine executes them over minutes. Each record carries the transfer id, direction ("outgoing" from this machine, "incoming" to it), the engine's own status, and state — the coarse verdict to read: "pending" (still in flight), "completed", "failed", or "rejected", with error carrying the reason for the last two. sourceTaskId is the task's id on the machine it left and localTaskId its id on the machine holding this record, which is how a moved task's two ids are tied together. A completed outgoing transfer is also when the source task closes. An empty list on the destination means nothing has arrived yet, never that a pull was not requested.

params.name: machine_id
params.description: Machine id from kanna_list_machines. Omit it, or pass the current machine id, to use the local machine connected to this client.

params.name: task_id
params.description: Task id (stable across stages) or one of the task's branch names (task-{id} or task-{id}-{n}).

tools.name: kanna_search_tasks
tools.description: Search Kanna tasks by case-insensitive substring match against display name and full stored prompt. Inside a task session this defaults to that task's repository; pass all_repos for the rare cross-repository search. Set all_machines for the existing account-wide result. Result rows carry only a prompt bounded to 500 characters, the latest durable agent name in agent, and the session transport in agentType.

params.name: machine_id
params.description: Machine id from kanna_list_machines. Omit it, or pass the current machine id, to use the local machine connected to this client.

params.name: query
params.description: Text matched (case-insensitive) against task display names and prompts.

params.name: repo_id
params.description: Repository id to search on one machine. Inside a task session this defaults to the caller task's repository unless all_repos or all_machines is true. Cannot be combined with all_machines because repository ids are machine-local.

tools.name: kanna_send_task_input
tools.description: Send ordinary input text to a Kanna task's live daemon PTY session as one logical message with its own Enter. Delivery is live-session-only and fenced to the PTY process ID observed before acceptance while holding the task's lifecycle lease. If raw desktop or mobile terminal input has opened an unsent draft, the daemon copies that draft off the composer, delivers this message on its own, and writes the draft back, buffering and replaying anything the human types mid-swap; when it can neither read nor verify that composer it instead queues the logical message FIFO until that draft crosses its next producer-declared submission boundary and fails with reason input_held_by_draft, which is now uncommon. The queue survives client/server reconnects and daemon handoff, but is never carried into a later run or stage. If no live input-capable agent session exists, or that session is replaced before acceptance, the call fails with reason no_live_agent_session and reports the latest run status and finish time when available; use kanna_resume_task to preserve provider context when possible, or kanna_rerun_stage to start fresh. An input_held_by_draft failure means a human has an unsent line at a terminal whose composer the daemon could neither read nor safely swap — an unmeasured provider, an inherited session, a dialog, or a draft it could not capture whole: the message was accepted into the daemon's queue but was NOT delivered, is not recorded in kanna_task_inputs, and will be written when that terminal submits — do not send it again, or a second copy will be queued. A delivery_uncertain failure means the daemon may already have accepted the message and it must not be retried blindly; one cause is a message whose text reached the composer while the terminal kept repainting, so its Enter was withheld and the text is parked there for a human. An input_blocked failure means the daemon refused to submit at all because it cannot prove what is on that composer — either it inherited the session and the composer holds text it never saw typed, or it parked a message there whose submission it could not prove; nothing was delivered, retrying changes nothing, and the target task now reports inputBlocked — report it and leave it to a human at that terminal. This can steer a merge singleton under its repo-defined policy. Every accepted delivery is recorded durably against the task and is readable afterwards through kanna_task_inputs, so a later stage can see what was instructed here; an uncertain delivery is deliberately not recorded. Set source to say who is speaking.

tools.name: kanna_send_task_raw_input
tools.description: Write discrete terminal keys, or explicit raw bytes, straight into a Kanna task's live PTY. This is the menu-driving counterpart to kanna_send_task_input, which cannot do it: that tool sends one logical *message* and the daemon appends its own Enter, so it can answer a question but never move a selection. Use this when a task's agent CLI is parked on something a sentence cannot answer — a selection list, a trust or permission prompt, a pager, a TUI needing Escape. Nothing is appended, nothing is wrapped in a bracketed paste, and nothing is queued behind a draft: the keys you name are the bytes that are written. Pass keys OR bytes, never both. EXAMPLES. Dismiss a dialog: keys ["escape"]. Move a selection down and choose it: keys ["down", "enter"] — written in that order, each acknowledged only after every byte reached the PTY, so consecutive calls also stay in order. Send an arbitrary sequence with no added newline: bytes "1b5b42" (hex, the default encoding; "G1tC" with encoding base64 is the same three bytes). ENTER. Only the named key "enter" declares a submission boundary, and a carriage return (0x0d) inside bytes is rejected for that reason: submission is a producer's declaration, never something read out of a byte stream, and an undeclared CR would leave the daemon's draft bookkeeping describing a composer that had already been submitted. Keys that only navigate, scroll, or delete create no composer text and so latch no draft; keys that type do, exactly as a human's keystrokes would. TERMINAL MODES. Cursor keys are the normal-mode CSI forms (up is ESC [ A). An application that has enabled DECCKM application-cursor mode expects the SS3 form (ESC O A) instead; most TUI parsers take both, some do not. home/end are CSI H / CSI F, backspace is DEL (0x7f), and function keys are deliberately absent because F1-F4 have two encodings in common use. Send bytes for anything this vocabulary does not spell unambiguously. DELIVERY. Discovery and delivery both hold the task's lifecycle lease, and every write is fenced to the PTY process ID observed during discovery, so a stage transition or rerun in between is refused rather than typed into the replacement. Success is 200 with status 'written' and a per-key writes list. Failures say what they are and carry a retryable flag; only one is ever true. 'no_live_agent_session' means nothing was written (there is no session, or it was replaced before the first key); 'raw_input_unsupported' means the running daemon predates this contract and nothing was written — restart the desktop app; 'daemon_handing_off' means the daemon is transferring the session to a successor and nothing was written, and is the only failure here that answers retryable true — make the same call again; 'session_operator_input_only' means a protected session accepts only kernel-authenticated operator input; 'delivery_uncertain' means the sequence stopped part-way or an answer was lost, so some keys may already be at the terminal — read the task's terminal, and do NOT resend, or the keys are typed twice. The writes list reports each key as written, uncertain, or not_written. AUDIT. Raw keys are not conversational messages and are deliberately NOT recorded in kanna_task_inputs: an arrow key is an action, not owner or manager speech, and the instruction history must not be readable as though it were. The action is announced on the task event feed as 'task.raw_input_delivered' with the exact bytes, class, and outcome of every write. SCOPE. This enables interactive menus. It is not an approval mechanism: deciding that a permission or trust prompt should be accepted is a judgement you are making on your own authority, and an unfamiliar prompt is a reason to ask the operator, not to press Enter.

tools.name: kanna_advance_stage
tools.description: Schedule a Kanna task to advance to the next workflow stage. The success response means the serialized transition was accepted; execution continues under the server's task mutation lease, and run.finished/stage.changed/task.closed events report the durable outcome or recorded failure. If the current stage declares a post, the post prompt runs in the current agent session first. A transition forks a fresh branch and worktree from the committed tip and starts the next stage's agent there; the task id stays the same. Advancing past the final stage closes the task. Declare source as operator for a human action or manager for a task-manager agent; the server records the declaration without authentication. Omission is recorded as unspecified, while engine policy transitions record auto. The stage this advance enters may be given an explicit provider/model/effort with next_stage_agent_provider, next_stage_model, and next_stage_effort — a per-advance override for that one stage, not a change to any workflow definition or default.

params.name: next_stage_agent_provider

The override applies to this transition only: it changes no workflow definition and no default, and later stages resolve normally. tools.name: kanna_push_task
tools.description: Send a Kanna task from the machine that owns it to another machine, preserving its prompt, durable delivered-input history, workflow stage, branches and committed work, and provider session, and closing the source task when the move lands. THIS CALL DOES NOT MOVE THE TASK. It queues an intent the server's transfer engine executes over minutes — bundling the repository, shipping the conversation, waiting for the source agent to wrap up — so the response always reports moved:false. state is "scheduled", "already_queued" (this exact intent_key was queued before), or "already_in_flight" (the task already has an outgoing transfer, reported in activeTransfer, and nothing new was queued). Read kanna_task_transfers for the durable verdict; never report a task as moved because this call succeeded. A push runs on the machine that currently owns the task, so pass machine_id to push a task that lives on a sibling machine, and name the destination with to_machine. The destination and its route are resolved and checked before anything is queued: an unknown machine, an untrusted or unreachable peer, or a cloud route whose credential the desktop app has not refreshed is refused with the reason and the fix, rather than scheduled and failed later on a relay socket.

params.name: transport

tools.name: kanna_pull_task
tools.description: Bring a Kanna task from another machine onto this one by asking the machine that owns it to push it here. THIS CALL DOES NOT MOVE THE TASK. It delivers a request the source machine turns into its own push, so the response reports moved:false with accepted:true and the source's requestId. That id is stable for repeats of the same pull within requestTtlSeconds, so an unchanged id — state "already_requested" — means the source is still holding the earlier request, not that a second move started. Read kanna_task_transfers on this machine for the incoming transfer, or kanna_get_task on the source task to watch it close. A pull always runs on the machine it moves the task to and therefore takes no machine_id; to move a task between two other machines, call kanna_push_task with machine_id set to the machine that owns it. The source and its route are resolved and checked here before the request is sent, and a cloud route whose credential the desktop app has not refreshed is refused with the fix rather than accepted; note that the source machine dials its own route back, so a cloud-routed pull also depends on that machine's credential being fresh.

guides.title: Kanna Repository Configuration
guides.summary: Repository configuration lives under `.kanna/`. Put committed, portable behavior in `.kanna/config.json`; put one-machine operational overrides in the gitignored `.kanna/config.local.json`. New config files should declare `"$schema": "https://schemas.kanna.build/config.schema.json"`.

sections.title: Schema declaration
sections.body: Set `$schema` to `https://schemas.kanna.build/config.schema.json` in every new `.kanna/config.json` and `.kanna/config.local.json`. Kanna publishes the schema with each merged version so editors and agents can discover supported fields and their semantics.

sections.title: Committed and local layers
sections.body: `.kanna/config.json` is the shared repository contract. `.kanna/config.local.json` is read from the open checkout's working tree, never from the origin snapshot, and is deep-merged over the committed file with local values winning. Local config may contain only `agentProviders`, `workflow`, `ports`, `setup`, `teardown`, and `test`; an unknown key, invalid JSON, or invalid value fails definition resolution and names the file. `agentProviders` and `ports` merge entry by entry, with a local entry replacing the committed entry of the same name. Every other permitted key replaces wholesale, and arrays never concatenate. Keep local config gitignored and do not put task-defining fields such as `vars`, `flavors`, `workspace`, `stage_order`, or reserved ports in it.

sections.title: Lifecycle commands
sections.body: `setup`, `teardown`, and `test` are arrays of shell commands run from the repository or task worktree. `setup` prepares each new workspace before its agent starts. `teardown` runs best-effort when a task leaves a workspace. `test` records the repository's canonical verification commands for agents and workflows. Because local arrays replace rather than append, repeat every command that should remain when overriding one of these keys locally.

sections.title: Ports and workspace values
sections.body: `ports` maps environment-variable names to base ports; Kanna reserves task-specific ports and exports the resolved values so parallel worktrees do not collide. `vars` provides committed string substitutions for agent prompts. `workspace`, `stage_order`, `reserved_ports`, and `reserved_port_offsets` are committed task semantics and cannot appear in local config.

sections.title: Workflow and flavors
sections.body: `workflow` selects the repository's default workflow by name. Kanna resolves a repo-authored `.kanna/workflows/<name>.json` before the bundled workflow of the same name. Workflow and agent definitions are public/listed by default; `visibility: internal` hides an effective definition from listings without preventing explicit resolution, and a repo override must redeclare it to remain internal. `flavors` selects a built-in variant by agent role (for example `"pr": "draft-pr"`); an explicit stage selector such as `pr@draft-pr` wins. Run `kanna-cli guide workflows` or call `kanna_guide {"topic":"workflows"}` before authoring a workflow.

sections.title: Provider, model, and effort resolution
sections.body: `agentProviders` maps exact agent names or `*` globs to a provider name or to `{ provider, model, effort }`; `provider` may be an ordered candidate list. Exact keys beat globs. Among matching globs, the most non-`*` characters wins and lexical order breaks ties. Selection precedence is: explicit task or stage override; matching `agentProviders` entry (including the local layer); layered `AGENT.md`/`EXTEND.md` frontmatter; global default provider. A rerun, resume, revision, or recovery reproduces the recorded run's provider as an explicit override, while a plain stage advance re-resolves the chain and uses the task's stamp only as the final fallback. Provider-specific model and effort values are layer-coherent: Kanna never combines them across providers or layers. It walks the same chain and takes the first value from a layer that would itself select the resolved provider. In an ordered provider list, model and effort belong only to the leading candidate; fallback candidates use a lower coherent layer or their own stamped/default values.

guides.title: Kanna Workflow Authoring
guides.summary: A workflow is an ordered set of stages stored at `.kanna/workflows/<name>.json`. Repo definitions override bundled definitions by name. Prefer selecting a maintained built-in in `.kanna/config.json` unless the repository needs different stages or policies.

sections.title: Definition shape
sections.body: A workflow requires `name` and a non-empty `stages` array and should declare `"$schema": "./schema.json"`. It may define `description`, named `environments` with setup/teardown commands, and `revision_limit` (default 5 agent-requested rounds; `0` means unlimited). Each stage requires `name` and `policy.transition` (`manual` or `auto`), and may set `agent`, `prompt`, `agent_provider`, `environment`, and a `post`. Stage and post `agent_provider` entries are compact provider selectors, `provider[-model[-effort]]`: a plain provider id (`codex`), a provider with a model passed to the CLI verbatim (`claude-fable`, `codex-gpt-5-codex`), and an optional trailing effort token (`lo`/`low`, `med`/`medium`, `hi`/`high`, `xhi`/`xhigh`, `max`) — e.g. `claude-fable-hi`, `codex-astra-lo`. Each selector in an ordered fallback list carries its own coherent model/effort pair; anything under-specified inherits the provider CLI's own defaults. Stage prompts support Kanna runtime variables such as `$TASK_PROMPT`, `$BRANCH`, `$BASE_REF`, `$PREV_RESULT`, `$PREV_MAIN_RESULT`, and `$STAGE_TRIGGER` (`auto`, `operator`, `manager`, or `unspecified`).

sections.title: Stages, transitions, and posts
sections.body: A manual transition waits for explicit advancement; an auto transition advances after the agent records successful completion. `policy.revision_transition` controls completion after entering that stage through a revision and defaults to `transition`. Advancing to an ordinary next stage forks a fresh branch, worktree, and agent session from the committed prior tip, so only committed work crosses the boundary. A stage `post` is different: it is tail work injected into the stage's running session before transition; its `agent` is the fallback if that session is dead.

sections.title: Visibility
sections.body: Top-level `visibility` is `public` by default. `internal` removes the workflow from listings and pickers but never prevents explicit resolution by name. Visibility belongs to the effective definition: a repo file shadowing an internal built-in must declare `internal` again to remain unlisted; omitting it deliberately promotes the workflow to a public choice.

sections.title: Built-in choices
sections.body: The public built-ins are `no-review`, `single-reviewer`, and `specialized-reviewers`, ordered by review depth, plus `plan-build-review`, which puts a manual `plan` stage in front of the `single-reviewer` shape so a human approves the approach before it is built. Every one of them carries implementation plus a commit post and ends with PR creation plus an approve post; only `plan-build-review` opens on a stage other than implementation. `specialty-review` and `architect-consultation` are internal workflows explicitly bound by orchestration; do not offer them as ordinary user choices.

guides.title: Kanna Agent Authoring
guides.summary: Agent roles live at `.kanna/agents/<name>/AGENT.md`. A repo `AGENT.md` replaces the bundled definition of the same name; `EXTEND.md` layers repository-specific changes onto the resolved definition without copying it.

sections.title: AGENT.md frontmatter and prompt
sections.body: An agent file is Markdown with optional YAML frontmatter followed by the prompt body. Common frontmatter keys are `name`, `description`, `agent_provider` (one provider or an ordered list), `model`, `effort`, `permission_mode`, `allowed_tools`, and `visibility`. Provider names and model/effort vocabularies are provider-specific. `permission_mode` is `default`, `acceptEdits`, or `dontAsk` (camelCase). The body is the instruction prompt and may use config and runtime variables.

sections.title: Overrides, extensions, and flavors
sections.body: A repo `.kanna/agents/<name>/AGENT.md` fully overrides the bundled agent of that name. Prefer `.kanna/agents/<name>/EXTEND.md` when the bundled behavior should remain and only repository-specific prompt text or frontmatter needs layering; Kanna reads extensions only from the open repo, never bundled resources. Built-in variants live under `flavors/<flavor>/AGENT.md` and can be selected through config `flavors` or an explicit `role@flavor` selector. An extension is role/flavor-scoped and layers after the resolved base definition.

sections.title: Provider coherence and precedence
sections.body: Provider selection is resolved before provider-specific model and effort. The precedence chain is explicit task/stage override, matching repo/local `agentProviders`, layered agent frontmatter, then the global default. Kanna takes model and effort only from a layer that would itself select the resolved provider; it never builds an invalid combination by borrowing values written for another CLI. In an ordered candidate list, values beside the list belong to its first provider only.

sections.title: Visibility
sections.body: Agent frontmatter `visibility` defaults to `public`. `internal` keeps the effective agent out of listings while explicit references still resolve. A repo override decides visibility for the effective definition, and `EXTEND.md` may override it.

guides.title: Kanna Task Operations
guides.summary: A task is a durable work item with a prompt, workflow state, run history, blockers, and a sequence of ephemeral workspaces. Prefer Kanna MCP tools for operations; use the instance-local `kanna-cli` only as a fallback.

sections.title: Identity and workspaces
sections.body: `KANNA_TASK_ID` is stable across stages. A normal stage transition forks a new branch and worktree from the committed tip, so commit everything that must cross the boundary. Do not infer task visibility from stage: `closedAt` determines whether a task is closed, and blockers come from blocker records. Do not push or open a PR unless the current stage explicitly asks.

sections.title: Completion and supervision
sections.body: Record a verdict with `kanna_complete_stage` when the stage prompt requires it; `success` may auto-advance and `failure` stops advancement. Use `kanna_wait_events` to supervise several tasks and `kanna_wait_task` for one. Read `runtimeState`, not blended `activity`, to decide whether an agent is busy, waiting, idle, or exited. `task.awaiting_input` is the positive interactive-question signal. Composer text is not an instruction unless its attestation is `typed`.

sections.title: Inputs and task terms
sections.body: Delivered input is durable and readable through `kanna_task_inputs`; terminal bytes alone are not the record. A non-zero `deliveredInputCount` means instruction history exists. Assess the task against its original prompt plus the durable owner, manager, and reviewer directives delivered during the task; do not require or invent a separate committed documentation artifact. `kanna_send_task_input` sends one logical message and the daemon appends its Enter, so it answers a question but cannot move a selection: an agent CLI parked on a menu, a trust prompt or a pager needs `kanna_send_task_raw_input`, which writes discrete keys (`keys: ["down", "enter"]`) or explicit bytes (`bytes: "1b5b42"`) with nothing appended. Raw keys are actions, not speech: they are announced as `task.raw_input_delivered` and deliberately never appear in `kanna_task_inputs`, so never read a menu keystroke as an owner directive — or the absence of one as proof a menu was never answered.

sections.title: Moving a task between machines
sections.body: A task can be moved to another Kanna machine, carrying its prompt, durable delivered-input history, workflow stage, branches and committed work, and provider session. `kanna_list_transfer_peers` names the machines this one can reach; a destination is a machine id from `kanna_list_machines` or a transfer peer id, never a display name. `kanna_push_task` sends a task away and runs on the machine that owns it, so pass `machine_id` to push a task that lives elsewhere. `kanna_pull_task` brings a task here and always runs on the destination, so it takes no `machine_id`. Both only queue an intent: they answer `moved: false`, and the transfer engine then bundles the repository, ships the conversation, waits for the source agent to wrap up, and finally closes the source task. Never report a task as moved because a push or pull succeeded — read `kanna_task_transfers` until the transfer reports `state` `completed` or `failed`. Routes are checked before anything is queued, and a cloud route is only usable while the signed-in desktop app keeps its credential fresh; that credential cannot be refreshed through this API, so a stale one is refused with the fix instead of scheduled.

guides.title: Kanna Mobile Previews
guides.summary: Read this topic with `kanna-cli guide mobile` or `kanna_guide {"topic":"mobile"}`. Make a task web app available with dev-server Preview on LAN, or share an HTML visual companion on LAN and through the authenticated relay. These are separate features; a localhost URL printed in the terminal does not expose a server to the phone.

sections.title: Dev server: declare, start, verify
sections.body: Declare the server's port in the repository's `.kanna/config.json`, for example `"ports": { "WEB_PORT": 5173 }` (see `kanna-cli guide config`). Kanna claims task-specific ports when creating the workspace and exports their values. Read `kanna_get_task` (CLI: `kanna-cli tool call kanna_get_task --arg task_id="$KANNA_TASK_ID"`) and check its `ports` array; use the claimed value, not the base number. Editing config or exporting a new variable alone does not claim a port for an already-running task. If the required port is absent, configure it before creating the next workspace and verify its task detail. Follow the repository's canonical dev command; for a Vite repository without a wrapper, an example is `pnpm exec vite --host 127.0.0.1 --port "$WEB_PORT" --strictPort`. Check `curl -I "http://127.0.0.1:$WEB_PORT/"` and the server log. Keep the process running for the user's preview and stop processes you started when finished, following the task's lifecycle instructions.

sections.title: Dev server: mobile access and limits
sections.body: Have the paired phone connect to the owning desktop over LAN, open this task, tap Preview (also in Task Actions), and select the declared web port if several are listed. The desktop proxies plain HTTP to `127.0.0.1` at that claimed port; the dev server need not bind to `0.0.0.0`. Preview supports HTTP and WebSocket forwarding, Refresh/Retry, and Open preview in browser (Safari on iOS). It is currently LAN-only: relay-only connections do not offer dev-server Preview. There is no public/shareable URL to generate and no need to manually create preview credentials. HTTPS upstreams and undeclared ports are unsupported. Response bodies are not rewritten: app URLs hard-coded to localhost, separate API ports, or HMR addresses can still point at the phone; prefer same-origin URLs and the dev server's own API proxy. If Preview is missing, check LAN routing, desktop support, and task port claims. If it reports not listening, check the selected claimed port and the local HTTP server. Closing the preview releases its session; closing the task or releasing its port invalidates access.

sections.title: Visual companion: publish task-owned HTML
sections.body:
In this task's current worktree, create `.superpowers/brainstorm//content/` and `state/` beside it. Write UTF-8 HTML to `content/screen.html` and a JSON metadata file to `state/server-info`; `{}` is sufficient for a file-only companion. There must be no `state/server-stopped` marker for an active session. For example, from the worktree root: ```sh companion_dir=".superpowers/brainstorm/mobile-demo" mkdir -p "$companion_dir/content" "$companion_dir/state" printf '%s\n' '

Design preview

Ready for feedback.

' > "$companion_dir/content/screen.html" printf '%s\n' '{}' > "$companion_dir/state/server-info" ``` Use a fresh session id or the existing companion tool's active session. Kanna discovers these files automatically; no dev-server port claim or HTTP server is required for mobile companion delivery. Existing companion tooling can continue to manage the same layout. The most recently modified eligible `.html` file across active sessions is selected, so update the intended file and retire stale sessions by writing `state/server-stopped`. Keep files inside the worktree without symlinks. A normal stage transition changes worktrees; runtime files left behind do not automatically publish in the new workspace.

sections.title: Visual companion: mobile rendering and feedback
sections.body: On the paired phone, open the task and tap Visual companion ready. Kanna streams the current document and subsequent updates over LAN or the authenticated relay. Use a self-contained HTML fragment or full document with inline CSS and inline JavaScript. Mobile blocks fetch/WebSocket connections, external scripts/styles, frames, form submission, and navigation; this is not a full dev-app browser. Keep source HTML within 1 MiB and images small. Supported local image references in the content directory can be inlined within size limits; do not rely on arbitrary filesystem paths or an asset server. For interactive choices use the companion's `toggleSelect(this)` helper on elements with `data-choice`; accepted click feedback is appended to the active session's `state/events` JSONL file. Read that file rather than assuming clicks arrive as terminal input. If the companion is unavailable, check the current worktree, server-info/server-stopped markers, newest HTML, file permissions, and content limits. Tell the user which task and mobile action to open, and whether you verified the rendered result or only the source.
